decision.summary: The Federal Reserve voted to keep the target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to 1/4 percent.

changes.quote: Information received since the Federal Open Market Committee met in April suggests that economic activity has been expanding moderately after having changed little during the first quarter.
changes.explanation: The Fed noted that economic activity picked up after a slow start during the first quarter.

changes.quote: The pace of job gains picked up while the unemployment rate remained steady.
changes.explanation: Job growth improved while the jobless rate held steady.

changes.quote: On balance, a range of labor market indicators suggests that underutilization of labor resources diminished somewhat.
Growth in household spending has been moderate and the housing sector has shown some improvement; however, business fixed investment and net exports stayed soft.
changes.explanation: Consumer spending and housing improved, but business investment and exports remained weak.

changes.quote: energy prices appear to have stabilized.
changes.explanation: The Fed acknowledged that falling energy prices have started to steady.

tone_quotes.quote: To support continued progress toward maximum employment and price stability, the Committee today reaffirmed its view that the current 0 to 1/4 percent target range for the federal funds rate remains appropriate.

The Committee anticipates that it will be appropriate to raise the target range for the federal funds rate when it has seen further improvement in the labor market and is reasonably confident that inflation will move back to its 2 percent objective over the medium term.

for_you.text: Card rates should not move on this decision; a $5,000 balance at about 11.98% APR costs about $49.92 a month in interest.

Mortgages track the 10-year Treasury yield, not the fed funds rate. The 10-year was 2.32% and moved 0 bp on the day; if that move passed through, the payment on a new $300,000 30-year loan at 3.87% would not change.
Savings yields should stay roughly where they are, since the Fed held rates.
Unemployment was 5.6%, and employers added an average of 237k jobs a month over the prior 3 months.

for_country.text: CPI inflation was 0% over the past year (May 2015); core PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, was 1.2%, against a 2% goal.
Real GDP grew at a 3.7% annualized pace in the latest reported quarter.
The 2-year Treasury yield, the most Fed-sensitive market rate, moved -4 bp on the day.
The broad trade-weighted dollar moved 0.01% on the day.

whats_next: The statement signals that the Fed will wait for further improvements in the labor market and more confidence in inflation before raising rates. As an educational note, the forecast model gave the next meeting a probability of 81 percent for a hold, 7 percent for a cut, and 12 percent for a hike.
